description: The ZeroZero turn raw space data into maps people can actually use. We’re a team of engineers and data people who believe the most powerful datasets are the ones you can see, explore, and act on.
summary: We built the Interplanetary Survival Guide, a 3D map of Mars that plans the safest trip across the surface for a crew with a rover. You turn the globe like Google Earth, over NASA CTX imagery at 5 m per pixel draped on 200 m terrain. Five data layers show what can hurt or help a crew: elevation and slope, ground firmness, surface temperature for any season and hour, buried water ice, and radiation dose. Pick a start and a destination up to 500 km apart, and the planner draws two trips, the safest and the quickest, driven as far as the rover can go and walked the rest. It lists time, distance, climb, coldest ground, radiation dose and each hazard, and it tells you when no route can avoid a hazard. An immersive view drops you 5 m above the ground at the spot you click. Mission planners, students and the public can see on one map which ground a crew could cross and which ground would stop them.
details:
What it does

The app is a 3D globe of Mars in the browser. One data layer shows at a time, each with a legend:

Topography: coloured elevation, plus contour lines from 2000 m down to 50 m intervals.

Ground firmness: thermal inertia in six classes, from loose dust that may not bear weight to bedrock.

Surface temperature: sliders for season and local time, daily low and high, and a 24-hour curve for the spot you click.

Water ice: polar surface ice and buried ice within 1 m, 1 to 5 m, and deeper than 5 m.

Radiation: modelled dose rate in Gale crater, terrain shelter, and the Curiosity RAD measurement.

Route planner

Set A and B by name, coordinates or a click. The server cuts the ground into 200 m cells and grades each one Clear, Caution, Danger or Extreme from slope, firmness and temperature, once for a person on foot and once for the rover. It returns a safest trip and a quickest trip. The crew drives where the rover can go (no slopes over 25°), parks on level firm ground, and walks the rest. If A and B connect only through hazardous ground, the planner marks that stretch unavoidable. If the trip exceeds the rover’s range or the walking limit, it shows the closest trip and the reasons it fails.

Immersive view

Click a spot and the camera drops to 5 m above the ground under a dusty sky. Six buttons move you across the terrain.

How we built it

Python (FastAPI, rasterio, NumPy, SciPy, Pillow) reads the datasets and draws map tiles on request. The frontend is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript on the ArcGIS Maps SDK, with no build step. We wrote our own thermal model of the ground and checked it against Curiosity’s REMS sensor: nightly lows agree within about 3 K, and afternoon highs come out about 11 K too cold. We anchored the radiation model to Curiosity’s RAD measurement. The app runs as one container on Google Cloud Run.

What we considered

Rover speed, range and walking limits come from NASA’s Space Exploration Vehicle concept, the Apollo rover and the EVA Walkback Test. They are planning numbers, and you can change range and walking distance in the panel. We state each layer’s limits in the app’s documentation: slopes average over 200 m, so the map misses short cliffs and boulders.

Benefits

A planner can compare landing sites by how far a crew can travel from them. A student can see why a 20 km trip on Mars may take a day.
